verdicts.summary: A second follow-up that steers into a follow-up run that is already being tracked does not create a duplicate task. A follow-up sent before the original result is published stays inside the original task.
verdicts.scenario: The original result is published. The user sends follow-up A, which creates run R1 tagged with task T1. Before R1 ends, the parent sends another message through MCP thread_send in auto mode, which steers into R1. message.runId is R1, and R1 already has a delegatedTaskId, so the code returns without creating a second task. I also tried an MCP sender that is not the parent: line 6779 returns.

verdicts.summary: I found no path that holds the child lock and then takes the parent lock, so the new parent-then-child order cannot deadlock against the paths I checked.
verdicts.scenario: I looked for a path that takes the child lock first and the parent lock second. handleTerminalRun takes the child lock and then the parent lock one after the other, never nested. recoverDelegatedTask runs from the effect worker or RestartContinuation and takes only the parent lock. ProviderEventIngestor takes the child lock only for provider_native children (line 412), and those never take this route. CheckpointRollbackService takes a single thread lock.

verdicts.summary: A task interrupted by a restart is not left stuck with a null result. The continuation run inherits the task's delegatedTaskId, so finalize and recovery settle the task from the continuation's run.
verdicts.scenario: Follow-up run R1, tagged with task T1, is cancelled when the server restarts, and a continuation is created. The continuation command skips recordSubagentFollowup (line 6761), but dispatchMessage copies delegatedTaskId from the run it continues. R2 therefore carries T1, and finalize picks R2 as T1's latest run. If the continuation is declined, recoverDelegatedTask finalizes T1 with settledContinuationOf.

verdicts.summary: thread_send reads the run from the projection after the command commits. The delegatedTaskId written in the same command is therefore present in the taskId it returns.
verdicts.scenario: MCP thread_send in auto mode queues a new run for a child whose result is already published. After dispatch, sendToThread reads the run again from the projection (ThreadManagementService.ts:636-644). That read includes the run.updated event carrying delegatedTaskId, which was emitted in the same command, so taskId is returned. A retry with the same clientRequestId gets the same commandId, so the derived taskId is the same.

verdicts.summary: A child can now have several tasks, and the web row keeps only one of them per child, the last one in the list. Stop still acts on the right thing, because it interrupts the child thread rather than a specific task id.
verdicts.scenario: The parent has an original task and a follow-up task for the same child. subagentsByThreadId keeps the last entry, so either task can back the row. If it is the original task, the newerRun check sees the follow-up's request time after the original's completedAt and shows the child's status with the result cleared. The Stop button calls interruptTurn with the child thread id, so it cannot stop the wrong task. The status mapping covers every value of OrchestrationV2ShellThreadStatus.

verdicts.summary: The SQL recovery query and the in-memory check apply the same two conditions. In SQL, a task row whose result is missing or null matches the in-memory `result === null` test.
verdicts.scenario: A task row has a null result and the child has a terminal run with that delegatedTaskId. Both layers select the child. I also tried a task that belongs to a different child but has the same id: the SQL query requires task.child_thread_id to equal the child, and the in-memory version filters on childThreadId.
